column2: Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate — describing the two-step assembly order: GPU and HBM bond to an interposer wafer, then the interposer wafer bonds to an organic substrate.

column1: How many DRAM dies are in a single HBM4 stack?
column2: 12 to 16 dies, stacked on a base logic die.

column1: What is the HBM4 interface width?
column2: 2,048 bits — double the 1,024-bit width of the original HBM generation.

What connects each DRAM die to the one below it in an HBM stack?
column2: Through-silicon vias (TSVs) — tens of thousands of vertical conductors piercing each die from top to bottom.

column1: What is the approximate interposer area for the H100-generation CoWoS-S versus Rubin’s CoWoS-L?
column2: ~2,500 mm² for CoWoS-S; ~4,700 mm² for the CoWoS-L variant used with Rubin.
Tiny copper-tin pillars that solder die to interposer at extraordinarily fine pitch, providing the high-density electrical connections between GPU, HBM, and interposer.

column1: Why is CoWoS called a 2.5D architecture?
column2: It is not fully stacked (3D) nor fully flat (2D) — dies sit side-by-side on an interposer rather than directly atop one another, capturing most vertical-integration bandwidth gains without the thermal problems of stacking compute on compute.

column1: Since when has CoWoS capacity been a binding constraint on AI hardware shipments?
column2: Since 2023 — NVIDIA’s CoWoS allocation is one of the most carefully negotiated quantities in the industry.
